The Mon city-states of Lower Burma, around the Gulf of Martaban, shown on the map in 900. The Mon were among the first peoples of the region to take up Theravada Buddhism and Indian writing, and their towns lived by rice farming and sea trade with India and Sri Lanka.

The best known were Thaton, near the coast, and Pegu (Bago), which tradition says was founded in 825. To the north lay the Pyu towns, then giving way to the rising Burman kingdom of Pagan. Across the hills to the east lived Mon kin in the Dvaravati lands of Thailand. Another label on the map, Mon state, shows the same people in other years.

Burmese chronicles say that in 1057 Anawrahta of Pagan took Thaton and carried off its monks, scriptures and craftsmen. Mon learning then shaped Burmese Buddhism and writing (Theravada at Pagan). The Mon rose again after Pagan fell, in the kingdom of Pegu (Hanthawaddy) founded in 1287.
